title: Transformers and the national grid
examTip: Transformers only work with AC. A changing current in the primary creates a changing magnetic field. This induces an EMF in the secondary. DC makes no change, so there is no induction. Always say this in transformer questions.
introTips: A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current. It does not work with DC.
Step-up transformer: more turns on the secondary → a higher output voltage.
Step-down transformer: fewer turns on the secondary → a lower output voltage.
The transformer equation is Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. The voltages are proportional to the numbers of turns.
The national grid sends electricity at very high voltage to reduce the current. Less current means less power wasted as heat.
intro: A power station might make electricity at around 25,000 V. By the time it reaches a pylon, it has been stepped up to 400,000 V. By the time it reaches your socket at home, it is back down to 230 V. Transformers manage that whole journey. The voltage changes are all about cutting waste. Sending electricity at high voltage keeps the current low. A low current means less energy is lost as heat in the cables. Without transformers, the national grid would waste so much energy that our electricity would cost far more. It would also be far less sustainable. Transformers are one of the most important practical uses of physics.

keyPoints.heading: How a transformer works
keyPoints.content: A transformer has two coils of wire, the primary coil and the secondary coil. Both are wound around a shared iron core. Alternating current (AC) in the primary coil creates a continuously changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field passes through the secondary coil. By electromagnetic induction, it induces an alternating EMF in the secondary coil, and so an AC. The core is made of iron because iron is a good magnetic conductor. It carries the magnetic field efficiently from the primary to the secondary. Transformers only work with AC. Direct current (DC) makes a constant magnetic field that does not change. So no EMF is induced in the secondary. If the secondary has more turns than the primary, the output voltage is higher (step-up). If it has fewer turns, the voltage is lower (step-down).
writeBullets: Primary coil → AC → a changing magnetic field in the iron core
The changing field induces an AC EMF in the secondary coil (electromagnetic induction)
Iron core — carries the magnetic field efficiently from the primary to the secondary
Only works with AC. DC gives no changing field, so no induction
More turns on the secondary → a higher voltage (step-up). Fewer → a lower voltage (step-down)

keyTerms.def: A device that uses electromagnetic induction to change the voltage of an AC supply; consists of primary and secondary coils on an iron core
The input coil of a transformer; carries the supply AC
The output coil of a transformer; carries the induced AC at a different voltage
The shared core of a transformer that channels the changing magnetic field between primary and secondary coils

keyPoints.memTip: Transformer = primary coil (AC in) → changing field in the iron core → secondary coil (AC out at a new voltage). It must be AC. No change, no induction.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People often say 'the transformer generates electricity'. It does not create electrical energy. It uses induction to pass energy from the primary to the secondary, at a different voltage.

keyPoints.heading: The transformer equation
keyPoints.content: The link between voltages and turns in a transformer is: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. - Vp = primary (input) voltage (V) - Vs = secondary (output) voltage (V) - Np = number of turns on the primary coil - Ns = number of turns on the secondary coil Rearrangements: Vs = Vp × (Ns/Np) or Np/Ns = Vp/Vs. Worked example 1: primary voltage = 230 V, primary turns = 100, secondary turns = 1000 → Vs = 230 × (1000/100) = 2300 V (step-up). Worked example 2: primary voltage = 11,000 V, primary turns = 500, secondary turns = 25 → Vs = 11,000 × (25/500) = 550 V (step-down). A transformer with more secondary turns than primary turns is a step-up transformer. Fewer secondary turns = step-down.
writeBullets: Transformer equation: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns
Step-up: Ns > Np → Vs > Vp (the output voltage is higher than the input)
Step-down: Ns < Np → Vs < Vp (the output voltage is lower than the input)
Rearrangement: Vs = Vp × (Ns/Np)
Units: voltages in V. Turns have no unit (they are just a ratio)

keyTerms.def: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns — the ratio of voltages equals the ratio of turns; used to calculate output voltage or turns ratio
A transformer where secondary turns > primary turns, giving a higher output voltage than input
A transformer where secondary turns < primary turns, giving a lower output voltage than input

keyPoints.memTip: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. Think of it as 'primary over secondary = primary turns over secondary turns'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to write the ratio upside down. Write it as Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. The same side of the transformer always goes together: primary voltage with primary turns, and secondary with secondary.

keyPoints.heading: Power in a transformer — the power equation
keyPoints.content: For an ideal (100% efficient) transformer, power in equals power out: VpIp = VsIs. Here Ip = primary current (A) and Is = secondary current (A). So if a step-up transformer increases the voltage, the current must decrease in proportion. That way the power is conserved. If a step-down transformer decreases the voltage, the current increases. Example: a transformer steps the voltage up from 230 V to 11,500 V (a 50× increase). The primary current is 20 A. Secondary current = (230 × 20) ÷ 11,500 = 4600 ÷ 11,500 = 0.4 A. The current fell by a factor of 50 as the voltage rose by 50. Power is conserved. Real transformers are not perfectly efficient. Some energy is lost as thermal energy in the coils, and in the iron core because of eddy currents. But GCSE calculations assume 100% efficiency unless you are told otherwise.
writeBullets: Power equation (ideal transformer): VpIp = VsIs
Step-up voltage → the current decreases in proportion (power conserved)
Step-down voltage → the current increases in proportion
Rearrangement: Is = (VpIp) ÷ Vs
Real transformers lose some energy as heat (eddy currents in the core). GCSE assumes 100% efficiency

keyTerms.def: The power equation for an ideal transformer — input power equals output power; voltage and current change in opposite directions

keyPoints.memTip: VpIp = VsIs. Both sides equal the same power (in watts). If the voltage goes up 10×, the current must go down 10× to keep the power the same.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is tempting to use VpIp = VsIs and Vp/Vs = Np/Ns both at once. Take each step separately. Find the voltage change first. Then use power conservation to find the current.

keyPoints.heading: The national grid — why high voltage?
keyPoints.content: The national grid is the network of cables, pylons and substations. It carries electrical power from power stations to homes and businesses across the UK. Power is sent at very high voltage (around 400,000 V), and so at very low current. The reason is that power loss in cables is given by P = I²R. The current is squared. So even a small cut in current hugely reduces the power lost as heat. For a cable with resistance R, halving the current cuts the power loss by a factor of 4. Stepping up to 400 kV makes the current tiny. So the power lost in the cables drops hugely. This makes transmission far more efficient. - Step-up transformers raise the voltage from the power station (~25 kV) to the grid (~400 kV). - Step-down transformers at local substations lower the voltage for homes (230 V) and factories (for example, 33 kV or 11 kV).
writeBullets: The national grid sends power at ~400,000 V (very high voltage, very low current)
High voltage → low current → less power wasted as heat in the cables (P = I²R)
P = I²R: power loss is proportional to current squared. Halve the current, and losses fall by 4
Step-up transformers at the power station: ~25 kV → ~400 kV
Step-down transformers at substations: ~400 kV → 230 V for homes

keyTerms.def: The network of cables and transformers that transmits electrical power from power stations to consumers across the country
Power lost as heat in a conductor = current squared × resistance; explains why high voltage (low current) transmission wastes less energy

keyPoints.memTip: High voltage = low current = less power wasted (P = I²R). The grid uses high voltage because current is squared in the power loss equation. A tiny current = tiny losses.
keyPoints.tutor_note: This is a very common 4–6 mark question. Give the full chain: step-up transformer → high voltage → lower current → P=I²R → less power wasted as heat in cables. Link each step clearly.

0.question: A student connects a transformer to a DC battery instead of an AC supply. What happens?
options: No EMF is induced in the secondary coil. DC makes a constant field, with no change to induce an EMF
The secondary coil produces a higher DC voltage
The transformer works normally, but less efficiently
The iron core magnetises permanently and becomes a strong magnet
0.correctFeedback: Correct! Transformers only work with AC. DC makes a constant (unchanging) magnetic field in the core. No change means no electromagnetic induction, so no EMF in the secondary.
0.wrongFeedback: Transformers need AC. DC gives a constant magnetic field. With no change in the field, there is no induction in the secondary coil. Without a changing field, no EMF is induced.

1.question: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 1000 turns on the secondary. The primary voltage is 230 V. What is the secondary voltage?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Vs = Vp × (Ns/Np) = 230 × (1000/200) = 230 × 5 = 1150 V. This is a step-up transformer, with more secondary turns.
1.wrongFeedback: Use Vp/Vs = Np/Ns → Vs = Vp × (Ns/Np) = 230 × (1000/200) = 230 × 5 = 1150 V. More secondary turns = step-up = a higher voltage.

3.question: Electricity is transmitted through the national grid at very high voltage. Why does this reduce energy waste?
options: Higher voltage means lower current. The power wasted in the cables is proportional to current squared (P = I²R)
Higher voltage makes the electricity travel faster, so there is less time to lose energy
High voltage reduces the resistance of the cables
Less electricity is used when the voltage is high
3.correctFeedback: Correct! P = I²R: the power wasted as heat is proportional to current squared. High voltage means low current. So I² is very small, and cable losses are kept low.
3.wrongFeedback: The key is P = I²R. High voltage → low current, because power is conserved (P = VI). A lower current → much lower power loss, because I is squared. This is why the grid uses high voltage.

commonMistakes: Thinking transformers work with DC. They do not. The changing magnetic field from AC is essential for electromagnetic induction in the secondary coil.
Writing the transformer ratio upside down. It is Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. The primary voltage always pairs with the primary turns, and secondary with secondary.
Forgetting that, for the same power, high voltage reduces the current. Power = voltage × current. If the voltage goes up, the current must come down to keep the power constant.
Saying 'high voltage reduces resistance in cables'. Voltage does not change the cable resistance. The benefit is a lower current, which reduces P = I²R losses.
Not linking the steps in a national grid explanation. Give the full chain: step-up transformer → high voltage → lower current → P = I²R → less power lost as heat in cables.
examTips: For transformer equation questions, write Vp/Vs = Np/Ns. Work out what you know and what you need to find. Then rearrange. Don't try to do it in your head.
Power equation questions: VpIp = VsIs. Find which side has the known current, then solve for the unknown.

National grid 4–6 mark questions need a clear chain of reasoning. Power station → step-up transformer → high voltage and low current → cables → P=I²R → less heating → step-down transformer → consumers.
Always say that transformers only work with AC, and explain why. A changing field induces an EMF. A constant DC field does not change.
In a step-up transformer, the voltage goes up and the current goes down. In a step-down transformer, the voltage goes down and the current goes up. Check your answer makes sense.
